distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: First-layer disease leaf for Enterococcus bloodstream infection across Enterococcus species. Species, resistance phenotype, source, healthcare acquisition, endocarditis, and shock are represented as mechanisms, axes, risk context, treatment modifiers, or event hazards rather than disease-name qualifiers.
distillation_scope.boundary_policy: E. faecalis, E. faecium, VRE, catheter-associated infection, biliary, urinary, intra-abdominal, endocarditis, septic thrombophlebitis, neutropenic, transplant, and shock presentations are context within this leaf or companion leaves, not appended to the disease name.
distillation_scope.ranking_note: Presentation-only ranking should use fever or blunted fever, chills, systemic inflammation, sepsis physiology, healthcare/GI/GU/catheter/source context, vitals, CBC, CRP/PCT/lactate/renal labs, and observed source imaging. Blood-culture species, VRE or ampicillin susceptibility, final echo confirmation, final source adjudication, treatment response, and follow-up outcome are confirmatory or post-workup context.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Portal or source entry into blood
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Enterococcus enters blood from gastrointestinal, genitourinary, biliary, intra-abdominal, catheter/device, wound, postoperative, dialysis, or initially occult sources.

Enterococci colonizing bowel, biliary tract, urinary tract, or disrupted mucosa translocate after obstruction, instrumentation, perforation, abscess, ischemic colitis, neutropenic enterocolitis, urinary infection, or recent antibiotics.

Density and persistence of viable Enterococcus in blood; drives positive blood cultures, recurrent bacteremia, inflammatory response, endocarditis risk, thrombus/device seeding, and treatment failure.

Host complement, neutrophil, monocyte, IL-1/TNF/IL-6, and acute-phase response to enterococcal bloodstream infection; fever may be low-grade or absent in older, renal, transplant, steroid-treated, or neutropenic hosts.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Host clearance impairment and healthcare selection
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Solid organ or stem-cell transplant, neutropenia, renal failure, dialysis, malignancy, steroids, diabetes, advanced age, central lines, prolonged hospitalization, and prior broad-spectrum antibiotics impair clearance and select for ampicillin-resistant or vancomycin-resistant enterococci.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Device biofilm and septic thrombophlebitis persistence
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Enterococcal adherence and biofilm on central venous catheters, hemodialysis access, urinary catheters, prosthetic valves, thrombus, or vascular grafts can sustain bacteremia and septic embolic phenomena.

Persistent enterococcal bacteremia can seed native valves, prosthetic valves, cardiac devices, vascular grafts, thrombi, and arterial lesions; E. faecalis bacteremia has a particularly important endocarditis search burden.

Undrained intra-abdominal or hepatic abscess, urinary obstruction or catheter, retained intravascular catheter, infected thrombus, biliary obstruction, prosthetic valve/device, perforated bowel, or ongoing mucosal injury continues bloodstream seeding despite active antibiotics.
Distributive shock, endothelial leak, hypoperfusion, AKI, encephalopathy, ARDS, DIC-like coagulopathy, and multiorgan failure from bloodstream infection, source burden, and host vulnerability.

Inactive empiric therapy, intrinsic cephalosporin resistance, ampicillin resistance, vancomycin resistance, daptomycin or linezolid non-susceptibility, high-level aminoglycoside resistance, subtherapeutic dosing, or toxicity-limited therapy prolongs burden.

mechanism_edges.rationale: A portal or infected source is the immediate route into blood.
GI/GU mucosal injury and colonization raise portal activity.
Impaired host defenses allow higher and more persistent burden.
Prior broad-spectrum exposure selects enterococci and VRE risk.
Viable burden raises probability of positive blood cultures; species identity remains confirmatory unless post-workup mode is tested.
Ongoing viable burden causes persistent or recurrent positive cultures.
Bloodstream infection triggers systemic inflammatory response.
Pyrogenic cytokines cause fever, though older, renal, steroid-treated, and neutropenic hosts may be blunted.
Reported fever often precedes measured fever at presentation.
Bacteremia frequently causes chills or rigors.
Fever, inflammation, hypovolemia, and shock increase heart rate.
Fever, acidosis, shock, pulmonary embolic events, or respiratory failure increase respiratory rate.
Subacute enterococcal bacteremia may present with nonspecific fatigue and malaise.
Leukocytosis is common, but neutropenia, transplant, marrow disease, or overwhelming sepsis can blunt WBC.
Neutrophil response depends on marrow and immunosuppression context.
CRP rises in invasive bloodstream infection and deep foci.
PCT may rise in bacterial bloodstream infection, though less stereotyped than gram-negative shock.
Inflammation, chronic illness, and capillary leak lower albumin.
Intra-abdominal, biliary, colonic, ischemic, abscess, or perforation source may present with abdominal pain.
Colitis, mucosal injury, enterocolitis, or antibiotic exposure can produce diarrhea.
Bowel ischemia, perforation, diverticular disease, neutropenia, surgery, or colitis disrupts mucosal barrier.
Colitis or ischemic bowel source may appear as segmental colonic wall thickening.
Enterococcal bacteremia often originates from urinary tract infection, urinary obstruction, catheter, or instrumentation.
Biliary obstruction, stents, or cholangitis can seed Enterococcus into blood.
Abscess, leak, postoperative abdomen, or perforation can seed enterococcal bacteremia.
Intra-abdominal abscess can be a nidus for persistent bloodstream infection.
Central venous access is a key healthcare context for enterococcal bacteremia.
Catheter biofilm or infected access raises catheter-source probability.
Persistent access-related infection raises infected-catheter probability.
Catheter or thrombus colonization can produce septic thrombophlebitis.
Septic thrombophlebitis can embolize to pulmonary arteries.
Uncontrolled abscess, catheter, urinary obstruction, biliary obstruction, or valve/device nidus requires procedural or device source control.
Uncontrolled source prolongs bacteremia.
Resistance, intrinsic cephalosporin inactivity, allergy, toxicity, or dosing problems lower active coverage.
Healthcare selection and VRE colonization increase probability of vancomycin resistance.
E. faecium and selected healthcare isolates may be ampicillin-resistant.
Cephalosporin-only or otherwise inactive empiric therapy can miss Enterococcus.
Persistent bacteremia increases opportunity for valve or endovascular seeding.
Endovascular seeding raises endocarditis hazard.
Vegetations can embolize to spleen, brain, coronary arteries, or lungs depending valve side.
Left-sided endocarditis raises systemic embolization hazard.
Sepsis physiology can lower systolic blood pressure.
Vasodilation and shock lower diastolic pressure.
Septic shock or mixed shock can lower MAP.
Hypoperfusion and mitochondrial dysfunction raise lactate.
AKI, CKD background, nephrotoxins, shock, and renal replacement context raise creatinine.
AKI, dehydration, dialysis, and catabolic illness raise BUN.
Sepsis, DIC-like coagulopathy, marrow disease, or linezolid exposure can lower platelets.
Sepsis encephalopathy, hypoperfusion, renal failure, or embolic events can alter mental status.
Hypotension, lactate, and organ dysfunction increase shock hazard.
Sepsis, aminoglycosides, vancomycin, CKD, and hypoperfusion increase AKI hazard.
Sepsis, fluid overload, pulmonary embolic disease, or respiratory infection can trigger ARDS.
Severe bacteremia can cause consumptive coagulopathy.
Organ dysfunction is the immediate early mortality pathway.
Delayed or inactive therapy prolongs burden and worsens outcome.
Uncontrolled source prolongs bacteremia and complication risk.
Endocarditis, embolization, valve failure, and endovascular infection increase mortality.

axes.shape_free_text: Probability that blood cultures are positive for bloodstream infection. Enterococcus species identity and susceptibility are confirmatory unless testing post-workup mode.
Duration of persistent or recurrent enterococcal blood-culture positivity once blood-culture follow-up is known; not required for presentation-only ranking.
Fever can be high, low-grade, intermittent, or blunted in advanced age, renal failure, steroid exposure, transplant, or neutropenia.
Patient-reported fever pattern before or during presentation.
Chills or rigors during bacteremia, including dialysis-session chills.
Tachycardia from fever, sepsis, pain, anemia, shock, or mixed cardiogenic physiology; may be blunted by beta blockade.
Tachypnea from fever, acidosis, shock, pulmonary embolic event, ARDS, or cardiopulmonary comorbidity.
Systolic pressure may fall with sepsis or mixed shock; some subacute cases remain normotensive.
Diastolic pressure falls with vasodilation or shock.
MAP integrates hypotension severity and vasopressor need.
Oxygenation may be normal or reduced from pulmonary embolic events, ARDS, heart failure, pneumonia, or fluid overload.
Subacute fatigue, malaise, dizziness, or constitutional illness.
Confusion, lethargy, coma, or encephalopathy from sepsis, uremia, shock, or embolic disease.
Abdominal pain from GI, biliary, urinary, abscess, ischemic, postoperative, or perforated source.
Diarrhea from colitis, mucosal injury, antibiotic exposure, or postoperative bowel disease.
Nausea or vomiting from abdominal source, uremia, sepsis, or drug toxicity.
Dyspnea from sepsis, pulmonary embolic disease, heart failure, ARDS, or cardiopulmonary comorbidity.
Chest pain may reflect septic embolic coronary event, pulmonary embolus, pleuritic complication, or competing cardiopulmonary disease.
Preexisting or new murmur increases endovascular evaluation context but is not required.
Leukocytosis is common, but leukopenia/neutropenia can occur in marrow disease or transplant.
Neutrophilia or neutropenia depending host context.
Neutrophil-predominant leukocyte response in non-neutropenic hosts.
Anemia may reflect chronic disease, renal failure, malignancy, inflammation, anticoagulation bleeding, or procedural complications.
Platelets may be normal or low from sepsis, DIC, marrow disease, renal disease, or drug toxicity.
CRP elevation from bloodstream infection and source inflammation.
Procalcitonin can rise in bacteremia and sepsis but may vary by source and host.
Lactate may be normal in subacute bacteremia or elevated in shock/hypoperfusion.
Creatinine reflects CKD, dialysis, AKI, shock, nephrotoxins, and renal dosing context.
BUN reflects renal failure, dehydration, dialysis, and catabolic stress.
Hypoalbuminemia marks inflammation, capillary leak, liver disease, malnutrition, or chronic illness.
Bowel ischemia, perforation, diverticular disease, colitis, surgery, neutropenic enterocolitis, or mucosal ulceration that enables Enterococcus translocation.
CT colitis or ischemic-colitis pattern that can indicate GI portal context.
Diverticula as a possible GI portal context, not a diagnosis label.
Bowel perforation hazard as source-control and mortality context when bowel leak/perforation evolves.
Probability that urinary infection, obstruction, catheter, instrumentation, or transplant urinary tract is the source.
Dysuria, frequency, urgency, flank pain, hematuria, or urinary discomfort when urinary source is clinically apparent.
Probability of biliary obstruction, cholangitis, biliary instrumentation, stent, or gallbladder source.
Probability of intra-abdominal abscess, leak, postoperative source, peritoneal source, hepatic abscess, or bowel source.
Drainable or persistent intra-abdominal, hepatic, perihepatic, pelvic, or postoperative abscess activity.
Central venous catheter, dialysis line, PICC, or comparable intravascular access present.
Hemodialysis catheter, fistula, graft, or dialysis access context.
Probability that an intravascular catheter or dialysis access is the source.
Probability that catheter biofilm or access infection is sustaining bacteremia.
Septic thrombus or thrombophlebitis related to catheter, vein, or endovascular surface.
Pulmonary embolic event from septic thrombophlebitis or competing thrombotic disease.
Need for catheter removal, urinary decompression, abscess drainage, biliary decompression, bowel repair, valve/device intervention, or debridement.
Adequacy of source control after intervention; a treatment/context axis rather than presentation evidence.
Recent broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure selecting Enterococcus or VRE.
Steroids, calcineurin inhibitors, transplant immunosuppression, chemotherapy, or other immunosuppression intensity.
Solid organ transplant immunosuppression context.
Profound neutropenia allowing GI translocation, persistent fever, and blunted inflammatory response.
Probability that current therapy has enterococcal bloodstream activity at adequate exposure.
Initial therapy unlikely to cover Enterococcus or resistant isolate.
Probability the enterococcal bloodstream isolate is ampicillin-susceptible.
Probability of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus phenotype, especially E. faecium in healthcare, transplant, dialysis, neutropenia, or prior antibiotic contexts.
Probability the isolate is treatable with vancomycin at achievable exposure.
Probability that high-dose daptomycin has active exposure against the isolate.
Probability that linezolid remains active against the isolate.
Probability that high-level aminoglycoside resistance prevents synergy.
Need to adjust beta-lactams, vancomycin, daptomycin, linezolid monitoring, or aminoglycosides for CKD, AKI, hemodialysis, or CRRT.
Severe beta-lactam allergy or immediate hypersensitivity limiting ampicillin or beta-lactam synergy regimens.
Baseline and treatment-emergent CK for daptomycin myotoxicity monitoring.
Hazard of infective endocarditis in enterococcal bacteremia, especially persistent E. faecalis bacteremia, prosthetic valves, prior valve disease, unknown source, or embolic signs.
Clinical or imaging activity of septic embolization from endocarditis or infected thrombus.
Hazard of systemic embolization from left-sided enterococcal endocarditis.
Hazard of septic or mixed circulatory collapse.
AKI hazard from sepsis, nephrotoxins, contrast, renal background, and aminoglycoside or vancomycin exposure.
ARDS hazard from sepsis, pulmonary embolic events, pneumonia, fluid overload, or shock.
DIC-like coagulopathy hazard in severe bacteremia or septic shock.

Lifespan outcome hazard driven by shock, AKI, ARDS, DIC, persistent bacteremia, delayed active therapy, VRE/MDR context, uncontrolled source, endocarditis/endovascular infection, age, renal failure, transplant, neutropenia, malignancy, and comorbidity.

axis_couplings.clinical_meaning: Fever and tachycardia often move together but beta-blockers and mixed shock can weaken coupling.
Inflammatory fever and CRP rise together with a short CRP lag.
WBC and ANC usually covary unless marrow disease distorts differential.
Leukocyte and acute-phase responses often align but can dissociate in neutropenia or steroids.
Worsening shock lowers pressure and raises lactate.
Renal dysfunction raises creatinine and BUN, with CKD background handled separately.
Renal dysfunction increases dosing and toxicity constraints.
GI barrier injury raises intra-abdominal source plausibility.
Intravascular access raises catheter-source plausibility but does not prove source.
Catheter-source bacteremia can seed thrombus or thrombophlebitis.
Persistent enterococcal bacteremia raises endocarditis hazard and need for echo evaluation.
Active therapy shortens persistence when source control is adequate.
Shock is a dominant early mortality driver.
Endocarditis, embolization, and valve/device complications increase mortality.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Ampicillin effect requires susceptibility and adequate exposure.
Severe beta-lactam reaction can preclude ampicillin.
Drug effect is weaker when abscess, line, obstruction, or endovascular source remains uncontrolled.

treatments.context_specific_role: Bactericidal beta-lactam backbone when isolate and allergy context allow.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Synergy requires ampicillin-active organism.
Endovascular high-burden contexts increase value of synergy.
Avoids aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity in renal impairment.

failure_modes: not sufficient for VRE E. faecium if ampicillin-resistant

side_effects.interpretation: Cephalosporin exposure can raise liver enzymes or cholestatic markers.

treatments.context_specific_role: Synergistic beta-lactam strategy for susceptible enterococcal high-burden/endovascular contexts while limiting aminoglycoside toxicity.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: High-level resistance prevents aminoglycoside synergy.
Renal failure raises aminoglycoside toxicity risk.
Existing AKI makes aminoglycoside exposure hazardous.

side_effects.interpretation: Ototoxicity risk with prolonged or high exposure.

treatments.context_specific_role: Synergy option when organism is susceptible and renal/toxicity context allows.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Vancomycin effect requires susceptibility and therapeutic exposure.
VRE phenotypes make vancomycin inactive.
Renal failure requires level-guided dosing.

treatments.context_specific_role: Coverage for vancomycin-susceptible enterococci when beta-lactam use is not possible or empiric coverage is needed.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Daptomycin activity requires susceptibility and adequate high-dose exposure.
Renal replacement therapy changes dosing interval and exposure.
Elevated CK or myopathy increases monitoring burden.

failure_modes: pneumonia source where daptomycin is inactivated by surfactant
treatments.context_specific_role: Susceptibility-dependent bacteremia option for VRE or beta-lactam-limited contexts with renal/CK monitoring.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Linezolid effect requires susceptibility.
Baseline thrombocytopenia increases linezolid marrow-toxicity concern.
Bacteriostatic therapy may be less reliable for high-burden endovascular disease.

treatments.context_specific_role: Active VRE option when susceptible, especially when oral bioavailability or renal safety matters, with caution in high-burden endovascular disease.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Tissue distribution may fit selected intra-abdominal source contexts.
Low serum concentration makes monotherapy unreliable for persistent bacteremia.
Susceptibility and combination context are important.

treatments.context_specific_role: Selected salvage or polymicrobial intra-abdominal context; should not replace active bacteremia therapy and source control when better options exist.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Procedure helps when a controllable nidus exists.
Complete source control shortens persistence.
Line removal can rapidly reduce access-related seeding.

side_effects.interpretation: Procedure bleeding risk depends on site and coagulopathy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Removal of infected line/device, drainage, urinary/biliary decompression, bowel repair, or valve/endovascular intervention when context requires.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Hemodynamic support matters when shock is present or imminent.
Support does not sterilize bloodstream infection.

failure_modes: persistent shock if antimicrobials/source control delayed

side_effects.interpretation: Excess fluid can worsen oxygenation in renal/cardiac dysfunction.

treatments.context_specific_role: State support while antimicrobial and source-control vector fields take effect.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Older adults can have low-grade or absent fever.
Bowel disruption is a key translocation context.
Abscess, leak, perforation, or colitis shifts source.
Drainage or repair may be needed.
Urinary tract is a common source.
Obstruction or catheter may require source control.
Enterococcus is common in healthcare-associated biliary infection.
Intravascular access raises catheter source probability.
Line removal or exchange may be required.
Enterococcal bacteremia with valve substrate or unknown source warrants endocarditis concern.
Immune or marrow status can distort WBC.
WBC may be low despite bacteremia.
Prior antibiotics and VRE context raise resistance probability.
Empiric regimens may miss VRE or Enterococcus.
Dialysis access context is present when applicable.
CKD raises AKI and drug toxicity risk.

supportive_care: Obtain blood cultures and source cultures before antibiotics when feasible, but do not delay therapy in unstable sepsis.

Treat blood-culture species, vancomycin resistance, ampicillin susceptibility, linezolid/daptomycin susceptibility, and high-level aminoglycoside resistance as confirmatory or treatment-context evidence rather than presentation-only diagnosis labels.

Search for source context: urinary obstruction/instrumentation, biliary obstruction/stents, intra-abdominal abscess or leak, bowel ischemia or perforation, central venous or hemodialysis catheter, wound, postoperative source, and initially occult GI/GU source.
Repeat blood cultures to document clearance and detect persistent or recurrent bacteremia.
Assess endocarditis risk with persistent bacteremia, unknown source, prosthetic valve/device, prior valve disease, murmur, or embolic phenomena; use echocardiography as post-workup evidence.
Use source control when indicated: remove infected lines, drain abscesses, decompress urinary or biliary obstruction, repair bowel leak/perforation, and manage valve/device/endovascular infection.
Adjust antimicrobial dosing and toxicity monitoring for CKD, hemodialysis, CRRT, AKI, thrombocytopenia, CK elevation, beta-lactam allergy, and drug interactions.
Provide sepsis support when needed: fluids, vasopressors, oxygen/ventilation, renal replacement therapy, lactate reassessment, and ICU monitoring.
quality_notes: No treatment-rank labels are encoded; treatment ranking should emerge from context axes and forward simulation.
Species and susceptibility are not required ranking evidence in presentation-only cases.
